title: Binary Search
summary: Halve the range every step, even on the answer

steps.title: Guess the number
steps.body: I pick a number from 1 to 100. After each guess I say higher or lower. Guess 50 first: whatever I answer, half of the numbers are gone in one go.

steps.prompt: 1 to 100, always guessing the middle. At most how many guesses?

steps.title: Same idea on an array
steps.body: Sorted array. Look at the middle: too small means x is to the right, too big means left. Each check halves what's left, so it's O(log n).

steps.prompt: About how many checks for 1,000,000 elements?
steps.why: 2²⁰ is about a million, so about 20 halvings.

steps.prompt: a = [2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38], x = 38. How many checks until it's found?
Why lo + (hi - lo) / 2 and not (lo + hi) / 2?
steps.why: Two indices near 2·10⁹ add up past INT_MAX. hi - lo never does.

steps.prompt: a[mid] < x, so x is right of mid
steps.why: a[mid] is already too small, so skip it. lo = mid can loop forever.

steps.prompt: a[mid] > x, so x is left of mid
steps.why: a[mid] is too big, so it's out. Only the left part can hold x.

steps.prompt: Put the search loop in order
steps.why: Find mid, check for a hit, then throw away the half that can't hold x.

steps.prompt: Binary search for 4 in [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]. What's wrong?
steps.why: Going left or right only makes sense when the values are in order.

steps.prompt: Match the size to the checks
steps.why: Every 1,000 times more data costs only about 10 more checks.

steps.title: NO NO NO YES YES
steps.body: Many problems ask for the smallest x that works. If x works means every bigger x works too, the answers look like NO NO YES YES. Binary search finds the first YES.

steps.title: Watch it run: find the first YES

frames.note: ok(mid) is YES. It might be the first, so hi = mid
NO. The answer is right of mid: lo = mid + 1
lo == hi. That's the first YES

steps.prompt: When can you binary search the answer?
steps.why: You need the NO…NO YES…YES shape. The input itself doesn't have to be sorted.

steps.prompt: ok(mid) is true. mid might be the answer, so keep it
steps.why: mid works, so it stays in the range. mid - 1 could skip the answer.

steps.title: Example: eating speed
steps.body: Piles of bananas and h hours. At speed k you eat one pile at a time, and a pile of p takes p / k hours, rounded up. Faster always works if slower does, so binary search k.

steps.prompt: What is (7 + 3 - 1) / 3 in C++ integer math?
steps.why: (p + k - 1) / k rounds up: 7 / 3 is 2.33, rounded up to 3.

steps.prompt: Piles [3, 6, 7, 11], 8 hours. Smallest k that finishes?
What's a safe hi to start from here?
steps.why: At that speed every pile takes one hour, so it works whenever any speed does.

steps.prompt: Why while (lo < hi) here, not lo <= hi?
options: With hi = mid, lo <= hi can loop forever
steps.why: Once lo == hi, mid = lo and hi = mid changes nothing. The loop never ends.
Keep mid when it works, skip past it when it doesn't.

steps.prompt: ok(x) is O(n) and x goes up to 10⁹. Total time?
Match what you see to what you do
steps.why: The range always holds the answer, and it shrinks every step.
